Cumhurbaşkanlığı bünyesindeki Dezenformasyonla Mücadele Merkezi (DMM), 10 bin Arakanlı Müslüman mültecinin Türkiye’ye yerleştirileceği iddiasını yalanladı.
Malezya Başbakan Yardımcısı Ahmad Zahid Hamidi dün (20 Kasım) sosyal medyadan ülkesindeki 10 bin Arakanlı Müslüman mültecinin Türkiye’ye yerleştirileceğini açıklamıştı.
İki hafta önce Türkiye’yi ziyaret edip İstanbul’da Cumhurbaşkanı Tayyip Erdoğan’la görüşen Hamidi bir süre sonra paylaşımını silmişti.
Malezyalı yetkili paylaşımında konunun Türkiye ziyaretinde gündeme geldiğini belirtip bakanlar kurulunun Arakanlı mültecileri ‘mesleki eğitim programı aracılığıyla’ Türkiye’ye yerleştirmeyi kabul ettiğini yazmıştı.
Malezya basınıysa süreçte Birleşmiş Milletler Mülteciler Yüksek Komiserliği (UNHCR) rol oynayacağını belirtmişti.
DMM bugün Reuters’e de haber olan iddianın ‘asılsız’ olduğunu duyurdu. X’teki kısa açıklamada ‘gerçek dışı içeriklere itibar edilmemesi’ istendi.
Birleşmiş Milletler verilerine göre Malezya’daki 190 bin mülteci ve sığınmacının 125 binden fazlası Myanmar’dan kaçan Arakanlı Müslümanlar.
Malezya, eylül sonu yaklaşık 1500 Myanmar vatandaşını, yetkililerin ‘gönüllü program’ diye tanımladığı süreçle ülkelerine göndermişti.
İnsan hakları örgütleriyse göçmenlerin, iç çatışmaların devam ettiği Myanmar’a geri gönderilmesinin onları tehlikeye atabileceğini savunuyor.
2017’de Myanmar ordusunun yürüttüğü operasyonlarda binlerce Arakanlı Müslüman öldürülmüş, 700 binden fazla kişi de nüfusunun çoğu Budist olan Myanmar’dan kaçarak komşu Bangladeş’e sığınmak zorunda kalmıştı.
Dünyanın en yüksek yargı organı Uluslararası Adalet Divanı (UAD), 19 Kasım’da Myanmar’ın Arakanlı Müslüman azınlığa soykırım yaptığına hükmetmişti. Bu, 1945’te kurulan UAD’nin bir devlet için aldığı ilk soykırım kararıydı.
Türkiye de UAD’nin bu hükmünü “Bu yargı kararını memnuniyetle karşılıyoruz” diye karşılaşmıştı.
Bazı uluslararası basın yayın organları ve sosyal medya hesaplarında yer alan, "10.000 Rohingyalının Türkiye’ye yerleştirileceğine" yönelik iddialar asılsızdır. Kamuoyunun, gerçek dışı içeriklere itibar etmemesi önemle rica olunur. pic.twitter.com/sF9wO0chLA

Haftaya lider giren Galatasaray, RAMS Park'taki çalışmalar nedeniyle Samsunspor'u Başakşehir Fatih Terim Stadı'nda ağırladı.
4. dakikada Galatasaray öne geçti. Sağ çağrazdan Batrakov'un kullandığı serbest atışta arka direkte Singo'nun dokunduğu top, Torreira'nın önünde kaldı. Uruguaylı oyuncu, altıpasın içinden yaptığı vuruşta meşin yuvarlağı filelere gönderdi: 1-0
42. dakikada Samsunspor gole çok yaklaştı. Coulibaly'nin sağdan ortasında Yunus Akgün'ün arka direkte kafayla uzaklaştırmak istediği top, altıpasın içinde Sekongo'nun önüne düştü. Bu oyuncunun bekletmeden yaptığı vuruşta, kaleci Uğurcan Çakır meşin yuvarlağı kornere çeldi.
47. dakikada Sara'nın ceza yayının solundan yaptığı sert vuruşta, kaleci Bilal Bayazıt gole izin vermedi.
53. dakikada Galatasaray ikinci golü buldu. Samsunspor yarı sahasının ortasında topla buluşan Sara, pasını şık bir şekilde ceza yayının sağından savunmanın arkasına sarkan Yunus Akgün'e verdi. Ceza sahası içinde kaleci Bilal Bayazıt ile karşı karşıya kalan Yunus, yaptığı aşırtma vuruşla meşin yuvarlağı filelerle buluşturdu: 2-0
57. dakikada Samsunspor, farkı 1'e indirdi. Mendes'in sağdan ortasında Bayo'nun ceza sahası içinde bekletmeden ayak içi yaptığı sert vuruşta, top kaleci Uğurcan Çakır'ın solundan ağlara gitti: 2-1
69. dakikada Sara'nın soldan kullandığı kornerde Abdülkerim Bardakcı'nın ceza sahası içinde yaptığı kafa vuruşunda, meşin yuvarlak üst direkten döndü.
76. dakikada sol kanattan ceza sahasına giren Tomasson'un yakın mesafeden uzak köşeye yaptığı vuruşta, kaleci Uğurcan Çakır topu kornere çeldi.
83. dakikada Emre Kılınç'ın uzak mesafeden çıkardığı sert şutta, Uğurcan Çakır gole izin vermedi.
Samsunspor, etkili olduğu kalan bölümde yakaladığı pozisyonları değerlendiremedi ve Galatasaray, karşılaşmadan 2-1 galip ayrıldı.
Teknik direktör Okan Buruk yönetimindeki Galatasaray, kulüp tarihinin Süper Lig'deki iç saha yenilmezlik rekorunu kırdı.
Sahasındaki son mağlubiyetini 19 Mayıs 2024'te Fenerbahçe ile oynadığı karşılaşmada yaşayan sarı-kırmızılılar, sonrasında Samsunspor maçına kadar lig mücadelelerinde 33 galibiyet ve 8 beraberlik alarak toplam 41 maçlık yenilmezlik serisi yakaladı. Samsunspor galibiyetiyle de bu seriyi 42 maça çıkaran Galatasaray, böylece iç saha yenilmezlik rekorunu kırdı.
Sarı-kırmızılı ekip, daha önce Süper Lig'de 2016-2017 sezonunun 32. haftasındaki Osmanlıspor mücadelesiyle başlayıp, 2019-2020 sezonunun 12. haftasındaki İstanbul Başakşehir karşılaşmasıyla sona eren 41 maçlık kulüp tarihinin en uzun yenilmezlik serisini yakalamıştı. Rekor seriyi o dönem turuncu-lacivertlileri çalıştıran Okan Buruk sonlandırmıştı.
Galatasaray, çıktığı son 7 resmi karşılaşmayı galip tamamladı.
Resmi maçlardaki son yenilgisini UEFA Şampiyonlar Ligi'nin 2. haftasında sahasında İspanya temsilcisi Barcelona karşısında yaşayan sarı-kırmızılı ekip, sonrasında Süper Lig'de 5, Avrupa'da ise 2 maçta puan kaybı yaşamadı.
Galatasaray bu süreçte Süper Lig'de Gençlerbirliği (1-0), Fenerbahçe (2-1), TÜMOSAN Konyaspor (4-0), Amed Sportif Faaliyetler (4-3) ve son olarak Samsunspor'u (2-1) mağlup etti. Sarı-kırmızılılar, UEFA Şampiyonlar Ligi'nde ise Fransa'nın Lille (4-2) ve Almanya'nın Stuttgart (2-0) ekiplerini yenmeyi başardı.
Sarı-kırmızılı ekip, Samsunspor ile Süper Lig'de oynadığı son 11 müsabakada 10 kez galip geldi.
Galatasaray, 25 Eylül 2005 tarihinde Samsun ekibini 2-1 yendiği maçla başlayan süreçte rakibiyle çıktığı 11 lig müsabakasında sadece bir kez mağlup oldu. Sarı-kırmızılılar, söz konusu tek mağlubiyeti ise geçen sezon ligin 32. haftasında 4-1'lik skorla gördü.
Söz konusu müsabakalarda 29 kez ağları sarsan Galatasaray, 17 gol yedi.
Sarı-kırmızılı ekip, Samsunspor ile sahasında oynadığı son 10 karşılaşmada puan kaybı yaşamadı.
Galatasaray, 24 Kasım 2001 tarihinde Karadeniz temsilcisini 2-0 yendiği maçla başlayan süreçte rakibini ağırladığı 10 maçın hepsinden galibiyetle ayrıldı.
Bu müsabakalarda 28 kez ağları sarsan sarı-kırmızılı takım, 12 gol yedi.
Galatasaray Teknik Direktörü Okan Buruk, maç sonunda ikinci sarıdan kırmızı kart gördü.
Maç biter bitmez sarı kart gören Buruk, itirazlarına devam edince hakem Ali Şansalan tarafından ikinci sarı karttan kırmızı kartla cezalandırıldı.
Buruk, ligin 13. haftasında Beşiktaş ile deplasmanda oynanacak derbide takımının başında olmayacak.
Galatasaray'ın Uruguaylı orta saha oyuncusu Lucas Torreira, bu sezonki ikinci golünü yine Başakşehir Fatih Terim Stadı'nda attı.
Torreira, daha önce 4. haftada yine bu statta oynanan İstanbul Başakşehir maçında ağları havalandırmıştı.
Galatasaray'ın milli futbolcusu Yunus Akgün, bu sezon 16. resmi maçında 4. golünü kaydetti.
Sezon başından beri 12 Süper Lig ve 4 UEFA Şampiyonlar Ligi karşılaşmasına çıkan Yunus, 3 kez ligde ve 1 kez de Avrupa'da rakip ağları sarstı.
Galatasaray'ın file bekçisi Uğurcan Çakır, karşılaşmada yaptığı kritik kurtarışlarla takımının galibiyetinde önemli rol oynadı.
Müsabakanın 42. dakikasında Samsunsporlu Sekongo'nun ceza yayı içinden bekletmeden yaptığı vuruşta kaleci Uğurcan Çakır, sağına uzanarak meşin yuvarlağı kornere çeldi ve skorun 1-1'e gelmesini önledi.
Uğurcan, 76. dakikada da sol kanattan ceza sahasına giren Tomasson'un yakın mesafeden uzak köşeye yaptığı vuruşta topu çelerek rakibinin beraberliği yakalamasına izin vermedi.
Milli file bekçisi, ayrıca 83. dakikada Emre Kılınç'ın uzak mesafeden şutunda meşin yuvarlağı önledi.
Galatasaray Sportif AŞ Başkan Vekili Maruf Güneş, Başakşehir Fatih Terim Stadı'nda oynanan karşılaşmanın ardından basın mensuplarına açıklamalarda bulundu.
Sözlerine ev sahipliği dolayısıyla İstanbul Başakşehir'e teşekkür ederek başlayan Maruf Güneş, "Zor bir zamanımızda yanımızda oldular. Başta Başkan Göksel Gümüşdağ olmak üzere tüm yönetim kuruluna teşekkür ediyorum. Bizi burada yalnız bırakmayan taraftarlarımıza da teşekkür ediyorum. Samsunspor'u da tebrik ediyorum. Bulundukları yeri şu anda hak etmiyorlar. Bence iyi futbol oynadılar, iyi mücadele gösterdiler ve bizi gerçekten çok zorladılar." ifadelerini kullandı.
Hakem Ali Şansalan'ın yönetimini eleştiren Güneş, şu görüşleri paylaştı:
"Futbol sahası, iki takımın mücadele ederek birbirlerine güçlerini gösterdiği bir arenadır. Ancak burası egosunu tatmin etmek ve rol çalmak isteyen kişilerin bulunması gereken bir yer değildir. Özellikle maçın hakemi Ali Şansalan'ın oyuncularımıza yönelik söylem ve davranışlarını kendisine yakıştıramadık. Maçın 52. dakikasında Mendes'in çok net bir şekilde ikinci sarı karttan atılması gerekirken kartını bu kadar cesur ve cömert şekilde kullanmayan hakemimizin, maçın sonunda teknik direktörümüz Okan Buruk'u ne kadar basit bir şekilde ihraç ettiğini bütün kamuoyu gördü."
Okan Buruk'un kırmızı kart görmesiyle ilgili yaşananları da anlatan Maruf Güneş, şunları kaydetti:
“Hocamız, kendisine çok yakın olan yardımcı hakemin elini sıkarak kendi yardımcısına yöneliyor. Orta hakemin elini sıkmıyor. Orta hakem de görüntülerde sabit olduğu üzere hocamızı ihraç ediyor. Akabinde Beşiktaş maçı olduğu için bunun hakemin bilinçaltında olduğunu düşünüyoruz. Hocamız kendisine 'Ben ne yaptım hocam sana?' diye soruyor. Hakem ise kendisine hiç yakışmayacak şekilde 'Savunmanı yazarsın' diyerek tünele yöneliyor. Bunu kendisine yakıştıramadık. Anthony Taylor acaba böyle mi hakemleri eğitmeye başladı? Gelen gideni aratıyor maalesef. Bu tavırlardan bir an önce uzaklaşmalarını, hakemlerin oyunculara, oyuncuların da hakemlere karşılıklı saygı göstermesini temenni ediyorum. Federasyonun, hakemin yaptığı bu ayıbı kapatacağını ve bu işin tamamen ortadan kalkacağını düşünüyorum. Biz gerekli başvuruları yapacağız. Çok haksız bir şekilde, çok ağır bir kararla bu ihraç gerçekleştirilmiştir. Bunun kesinlikle ortadan kaldırılmasını talep edeceğiz. Takdir yine Türkiye Futbol Federasyonunundur.”
Bu sezon Süper Lig'de üst üste 5. şampiyonluğu hedeflediklerini belirten Güneş, "Biz 4 yıldır bu işi göğüsledik. Şu anda da en yakın rakiplerimize çok ciddi puan farkları atmış durumdayız. Beşinci şampiyonluğa emin adımlarla gidiyo…

Başkan Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, "Haklıya hakkının teslim edilmediği, kanunların hakkaniyetle uygulanmadığı, zalimin, zorbanın, suçlunun işlediği cürmün cezasını çekmediği bir düzende huzur, güvenlik, toplumsal birlik sağlanamaz. Toplumun bütün kesimlerine güven veren, doğru, adil ve etkili işleyen bir yargı sistemi, toplumsal huzur ve barışın anahtarıdır" dedi.
Başkan Erdoğan, Eyüpsultan'daki Gaziosmanpaşa Adalet Sarayı'nın resmi açılış töreninde katılımcıları selamlayarak başladığı konuşmasında, eser ve hizmet siyasetine yeni bir halka eklemenin bahtiyarlığı içerisinde olduklarını söyledi. Yeni adalet sarayının İstanbul, yargı teşkilatı ve millet için hayırlara vesile olmasını dileyen Erdoğan, daha önce üç ayrı binada hizmet veren Gaziosmanpaşa Adliyesi ile ek binaların tek çatı altında birleştirildiğini dile getirdi. Bunu yaparken adalet hizmetlerinin daha etkin, daha hızlı, sunulan hizmetin saygınlığına uygun şekilde verilmesini hedeflediklerini vurgulayan Erdoğan, şöyle konuştu:
"Hakimlerimiz, savcılarımız, avukatlarımız aynı şekilde adliye personelimizin tamamı görevlerini daha iyi koşullarda yerine getirsin, altyapıdan kaynaklı hiçbir sorunla karşılaşmasın istedik. Taşınma işlemlerinin sona ermesiyle birlikte yeni hizmet binamız faaliyete geçti. Gaziosmanpaşa Adalet Sarayı modern ve işlevsel yapısıyla gerçekten göz dolduruyor. Yaklaşık 90 bin metrekare kapalı alana sahip bu bina 7'si bodrum katı, 21'i normal kat ve bir çatı katı olmak üzere toplam 29 kattan oluşuyor. Binada 160 adet cumhuriyet savcısı odası, 136 adet hakim odası ve 14 adet ağır ceza mahkemesi başkanı odası var. 113 adet duruşma salonuna ilave olarak toplamda 360 kişilik iki büyük duruşma salonumuz bulunuyor. Ayrıca 317 araçlık otopark alanı da burada hizmet verecek. Sağlık ünitesinden market ve mağazaya, postane ve banka şubesinden sosyal yaşam alanlarına buradaki her bölüm yüksek bir kalite standardıyla hizmet sunacak."
Yeni adliye binasının iç mekan tasarımının çağdaş, adli hizmetlere uyumlu olarak düzenlendiğini dile getiren Erdoğan, "Ön bürolar ve duruşma salonları ileri teknolojili bilişim altyapısıyla donatıldı. Yargı alanı Gaziosmanpaşa, Sultangazi, Eyüpsultan ve Arnavutköy ilçelerimizdeki 1 milyon 791 bin kişiyi kapsayan yeni adliyemizin bir kez daha hayırlı uğurlu olmasını diliyorum." diye konuştu. Yeni adalet sarayının yapımında emeği bulunanları tebrik eden Erdoğan, "Bu çatı altında görev yapacak hakimlerimizin ve cumhuriyet savcılarımızın, avukatlarımızın ve adliye personelimizin insan odaklı adalet anlayışıyla milletimize en yüksek standartta hizmet sunacağına inanıyorum." dedi.
Başkan Erdoğan, "Toplumları ve devletleri güçlü kılan, her şeyden önce adalettir. Merkezinde adaletin olmadığı hiçbir sistem yaşama imkanı bulamaz. Haklıya hakkının teslim edilmediği, kanunların hakkaniyetle uygulanmadığı, zalimin, zorbanın, suçlunun işlediği cürmün cezasını çekmediği bir düzende huzur, güvenlik, toplumsal birlik sağlanamaz. Toplumun bütün kesimlerine güven veren, doğru, adil ve etkili işleyen bir yargı sistemi, toplumsal huzur ve barışın anahtarıdır." ifadelerini kullandı.
Başkan Erdoğan, merhum şair Niyazi Yıldırım Gençosmanoğlu'nun adaletin ertelenemez bir ihtiyaç olduğunu, "Ekmek, su, aş bulmak gecikebilir. Temele taş bulmak gecikebilir. Devlete baş bulmak gecikebilir. Adalet gecikmez, tez verilmeli." sözleriyle anlattığını belirterek, şunları ifade etti: "İşte bizim tüm çabamız, tüm gayemiz bugün burada olduğu gibi bütün yatırımlarımız, adaletin gecikmeden tecelli etmesi içindir. Adli ve idari yargıda yaptığımız reformların, düzenlemelerin, kanun değişikliklerinin ve dijital dönüşümün odağında diğer pek çok hedefle birlikte yargılama sürelerinin kısaltılması vardır. Adalet Bakanlığımızın son dönemde hayata geçirdiği ALO Adalet gibi, davalarda hedef süre uygulamalarının sıkı takibi gibi adımlar yine buna yöneliktir."
Yeni adalet saraylarının inşasını, mevcut adalet binalarının teknik ve fiziki koşullarının iyileştirilmesini çok önemli gördüklerini kaydeden Erdoğan, "Yargı faaliyetlerinin yerine getirildiği binaların gerek mimari gerek tefrişat gerekse teknik donanım açısından yeterli şartlara sahip olması için ne gerekiyorsa yapıyoruz. Hükümetlerimiz döneminde adliyelerimizi teknolojik araç ve ekipmanlarla güçlendirdik. Adalet hizmet binalarımızı çağın ihtiyaçlarını karşılayan, engelli vatandaşlarımızın rahatça istifade edebilecekleri bir yapıya kavuşturduk. Erişilebilirlik kriterlerini hem halihazırdaki adliyelerimizde hem de yeni inşa ettiğimiz binalarda titizlikle uyguladık." ifadelerini kullandı. "ÜMRANİYE'DE YAKLAŞIK 200 BİN METREKARELİK YENİ BİR ADLİYE İNŞA ETMEYİ HEDEFLİYORUZ" Başkan Erdoğan, rakamların bu konudaki hassasiyetlerini çok net biçimde ortaya koyduğunu belirterek, şu verileri paylaştı:
"24 yıl önce sadece 569 bin metrekare olan adalet hizmet binalarının kapalı kullanım alanını yaptığımız yatırımlarla 10 kattan fazla artırarak tam 6 milyon 191 bin metrekareye ulaştırdık. 2002'den bugüne Türkiye genelinde 306 adet adliye hizmet binası için 226 milyar 830 milyon liranın üzerinde harcama yaptık. Daha önce hastanelerde elverişsiz şartlarda hizmet veren adli tıp kurumlarını ileri teknolojiye sahip, yeni ve müstakil hizmet binalarına taşıdık. Aynı dönemde adalet hizmetlerini geliştirmek için yalnızca İstanbul'da 43 milyar 494 milyon liralık yatırım yaptık." Küçükçekmece, Kadıköy, Çatalca, Bakırköy, Silivri, İstanbul Çağlayan ve İstanbul Anadolu adalet saraylarını şehre kazandırdıklarını aktaran Erdoğan, "İstanbul Bölge İdare Mahkemesi ve İstanbul Bölge Adliye Mahkemesi'ni inşa ederek vatandaşlarımızın kullanımına sunduk. İstanbul Adli Tıp Binası, Kartal Adalet Binası ve Bakırköy Adalet Binası Sosyal Tesisi'ni ise restorasyona tabi tutarak dönüştürdük. Ceza infaz kurumları ve çocuk eğitim merkezlerinden oluşan 14 yeni yapıyı da aynı şekilde tamamlayarak hizmete aldık." diye konuştu. Başkan Erdoğan, "İstanbul Adli Tıp Grup Başkanlığı hizmet binasının inşası devam ediyor. Onu da inşallah 2028'de tamamlayıp faaliyete alacağız. Proje aşaması sona eren Büyükçekmece Adalet Binası'nın ihalesini de gerçekleştirerek yapımına başlayacağız." dedi. Çağlayan Ek Adalet Binası için adliyeye yakın mesafede 300 bin metrekare kullanım alanına sahip yeni bir bina yapmayı planladıklarını kaydeden Erdoğan, "Artan dosya sayısı nedeniyle İstanbul Anadolu Adliyesi'nin fiziken artık yetersiz kalmaya başladığını görüyoruz. Bunun önüne geçebilmek amacıyla Ümraniye ilçemizde yaklaşık 200 bin metrekarelik yeni bir adliye inşa etmeyi hedefliyoruz." ifadelerini kullandı. Başkan Erdoğan, "Adalet hizmetlerinin daha nitelikli sunulması, vatandaşlarımızın bu hizmetlere daha hızlı ulaşabilmesi, gecikmelerin ve mağduriyetlerin önüne geçilebilmesi için bundan sonra da kararlılıkla çalışmaya devam edeceğiz." diye konuştu.
"YARGIMIZ İÇİN EMANETİN HAKKINI VERMEK ADLİYENİN KAPISINI, ADALETİN KAPISI HALİNE GETİREREK OLUR" Modern, geniş, konforlu mekanların hizmetlerin ifasında kuşkusuz önemli olduğunu ancak binaların insanla anlam kazandığını aktaran Erdoğan, "Gerçek misyonunu insanla icra eder. Cam, çelik ve betondan müteşekkil bu yapıyı gerçek manada bir adalet sarayına çevirecek olan sizlerin gayretleridir, emekleridir, çalışmalarıdır. Özellikle adalet hizmetlerinde aslolan mesuliyet sahiplerinin devlete ve millete karşı sorumluluklarını layıkıyla yerine getirmesidir. Konumu, ünvanı, makamı ne olursa olsun bir kamu görevlisinin ilk vazifesi milletin emanetinin hakkını vermektir." sözlerini sarf etti.
Başkan Erdoğan, şunları kaydetti: "Yargımız için emanetin hakkını vermek ise adliyenin kapısını, adaletin kapısı haline getirerek olur. Zengin fakir ayırt etmeksizin, bu kapıyı özellikle kapıya gelen herkese hakkına erişeceğini hissettirmekle olur. The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.
When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.
"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.
This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
A mathematician at Anthropic has convincingly said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.
On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.
The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.
“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.
Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution.
“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced.
Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”
The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.
The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.
Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.
Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.
In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.
Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.
University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.
He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”
texts.https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/g-s1-1549:
Paul Smith, chief commercial officer of Anthropic, center left, and Krishna Rao, chief financial officer of Anthropic, center right, alongside others react during the closing bell ceremony for the Anthropic IPO at Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Seth Wenig/AP hide caption
A mathematician who works for artificial intelligence giant Anthropic claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of the company's AI tool Claude.
It marks the second time in recent months that an AI company or someone linked to one claims to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem.
Levent Alpöge, a member of the company's technical staff, made the announcement Friday by way of a four-page explanation posted on his website. He said that he believes by working with Claude, he has found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in 1859, the Riemann Hypothesis centers on the distribution of prime numbers — those that are only divisible by one and themselves — as they grow towards infinity.
Alpöge said his discovery came late Sunday night. He messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about "my ability to announce," as the San Francisco-based company was about to make major news with its stock market debut.
A day after the company's initial public offering — the most valuable in history — Alpöge revealed he'd solved the problem that has proved elusive for more than 150 years. Anthropic did not respond to an email from The Associated Press requesting comment on Alpöge's claim.
Alpöge released his and Claude's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis within 17 million lines of Lean code, a programing language that allows people to program proofs of mathematical theorems. Traditionally the findings buried in that code would be published in a formal paper, said Alex Kontorovich, distinguished professor and department chair of mathematics at Rutgers University.
"Usually when somebody gives you a paper, that's also kind of code for a proof and you have to actually read the paper, follow it yourself, figure out if you believe every single line in that paper. And when you're done, you should have a deep understanding of why something is true," he said.
He said Claude followed that code and said the proof is true.
"Does that mean I understand it? Not yet. But the computer is extraordinarily picky, way pickier than I am and so if you can satisfy the computer, there's a very, very good chance you're going to satisfy me too," he said. "But I have to do the work."
Hours after the announcement, the Riemann Hypothesis remained listed as unsolved on the Clay Mathematics Institute's website. The institute had selected the hypothesis back in 2000 as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered a reward of $1 million for the solution.
The assessment process of whether the problem has actually been solved takes time, explained Martin Bridson, president of the institute.
"This is an announcement of historic significance, which holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics," he said in a statement. "But the journey from today's announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
Alpöge said he is "presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics." He said more than 250,000 pages came out of his work with AI.
In September, OpenAI said its technology was key in a similar breakthrough with Navier-Stokes, an equation that governs the flow of fluids.
"Navier-Stokes fell and now the Riemann Hypothesis," said Kontorovich. "There's some kind of out-of-body experience where I'm looking at myself saying, 'Yes, the Riemann Hypothesis has been solved,' and kind of trying to comprehend what the hell these words are coming out of my mouth."
Anthropic made a blockbuster Wall Street debut this week, through which it raised a record-breaking $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation.
Amodei has projected an optimistic vision for AI's future in which the technology leads to significant advancements in math and science research while simultaneously warning about the potential risks AI poses.

"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."

Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons.
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”
Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine , Gaza , and Sudan.
According to NPR , Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

We rely on US tech platforms to provide the digital infrastructure of daily life. What happens when they all go dark?
Sovereignty has become the buzzword of political rhetoric at precisely the moment it has become harder than ever to define, let alone control, and most Australians feel unsafe in the world .
It is a word that regularly trips off the prime minister’s tongue as he jets around the world to global forums.
At these gatherings leaders of proud but worried nations try to recalibrate how to deal with the old superpower. One that has become, in a phrase Canada’s trade minister, Chrystia Freeland, used as the title of her new book, an “unreliable boyfriend”. She describes a partner who became a bully . Coercive control at a global level takes many forms.
Once sovereignty would have been defined by territory, shaped by governments, reinforced by armies, strong institutions, electoral systems and a robust culture. Those are all still important but have been undermined.
Monopolistic global platforms now provide the infrastructure of daily life, defence, commerce, public administration, education, media, culture and everything else. Cory Doctorow graphically describes this chilling capture in his book Enshitification and, although he is hopeful that this can be reversed, it will be a tough fight .
Even with the best regulatory systems imaginable this digital infrastructure, shaped by commercial imperatives and protected and reinforced by the unreliable boyfriend’s laws and institutions, is not within national control. The prime minister likes to boast about Australia as a world leader in digital sovereignty, citing the social media ban for under-16s – an important , but very limited, first step. In practice what sounded like sovereignty feels more like accommodation.
When Microsoft went dark last week the wheels of government, commerce and ordinary life ground to a halt. At least half a billion people were directly affected – all at once and all around the world. Economies were paralysed.
At first it seemed like a bit of a joke but then the reality dawned. Microsoft Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint, Defender XDR control the fabric of modern life – email, calendars, meetings, access to files and documents.
Just the week before, David Thodey, the University of Sydney’s chancellor and a former head of CSIRO and Telstra, posed a question at a Royal Society forum considering the tipping points of existential risk. He wondered about the sovereign risk Australia faced by relying so absolutely on US technology platforms for defence and cloud services. “What would happen if Microsoft, Salesforce, Google and Anthropic all went down?” he asked.
The answer required a much bigger debate than we are accustomed to – about national priorities, money, ambition and delivery.
Anthony Albanese had raised a similar concern with unusual precision when he launched his approach to AI policy, saying : “If we are always dependent on someone, somewhere else, we will always be vulnerable.”
Although there has been a lot of noise since, it is unclear that the underlying sovereignty problem is being adequately addressed .
Accommodating the tech giants without giving too much away seems to be the focus.
There is an inclination to give up, as Greg Sheridan wrote in The Australian : “There is almost nothing Australia can do.”
The creative community is spearheading a campaign to address the fundamental cultural issue – the theft of copyright material to train AI models. The digital duty of care inquiry is highlighting the vulnerability of businesses which can be unilaterally removed from the platform they depend on. The research community is pointing to the catastrophic underfunding of Australian research and development.
This is not just an Australian problem. There are lessons from elsewhere, as the University of Melbourne research fellow Andrew Cullen noted : “By actively funding decentralised cloud infrastructure and homegrown software, European governments are ensuring that an American tech failure cannot knock out a local hospital. The world must adopt a similar blueprint.”
Instead, the Australian government is strengthening ties with its unreliable boyfriend. It is pouring buckets of money into a submarine and defence infrastructure project that will reshape the Australian military and economy for generations.
The links between defence and AI cannot be underestimated. As they entwine, sovereignty will become more elusive.
Aukus is already skewing industry policy towards creating military industrial research and enterprises. US anti-trans employment policies undermine Australian defence employment policy. Immunising defence sites from local laws and criminalising photographing military sites would revoke established freedoms.
The independent inquiry into Aukus concluded that the $368bn agreement is a deception that threatens to surrender Australian sovereignty .
The government did not but in the inquiry but a thousand others did, including eminent experts, former prime ministers, ministers, generals, admirals and ambassadors. They can’t all be wrong. The failure to engage and take part in a robust debate highlights a sovereign vulnerability.
The Australian National University’s National Security College released a survey this year that showed that Australians were worried about security and wanted more money spent at home to provide greater resilience .
The inquiry’s Surrendering Australia report showed that the billions allocated to Aukus could instead fund 44 conventional submarines, 180 major hospitals, 1.47m homes, upgrade every public school, eight years of the national disability insurance scheme, and solar power and batteries for every home.
We should at least have an open debate about whether that would strengthen resilience and sovereignty more than dependence on an unreliable boyfriend.

Sultangazi İlçe Emniyet Müdürlüğü ekiplerinin yaptığı incelemede, cesedin yaklaşık 3-4 günlük olduğu ve başında darp izi bulunduğu yönündeki bulgular nedeniyle ilk aşamada cinayet ihtimali üzerinde duruldu.
Ancak adli tıp incelemesinde kişinin düşmeye bağlı boyun kırığı sonucu hayatını kaybettiği değerlendirildi. Hayatını kaybeden kişinin kimliği henüz belirlenemezken, ülkeye yasa dışı yollarla giriş yapmış olabileceği ihtimali üzerinde duruluyor. Olayla ilgili başlatılan soruşturma sürüyor.
Olay sırasında sokakta bulunan Rüveyda D., "Saat 23.00 sıralarında polis ekipleri geldi. Sorduğumuzda, ceset bulunduğunu ve büyük ihtimalle cinayet olduğunu söyledi.

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.
According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”
Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.
Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.
Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion.
The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.
In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls .
Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.
It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.
It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.
Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.
Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.
The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.
South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.
The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.
The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”
Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.
The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.
Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.
Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”
A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.
On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

An armed robot developed by Turkish defense companies is demonstrated at a facility in Duzce, Turkey, on April 29. Omer Urer/Anadolu via Getty Images hide caption
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.
Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.
Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate," and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to "pushing the can down the road for two more years."
They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: "States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities."
Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.
"Technology is moving faster than diplomacy," said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. "Diplomats are very slow."
After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn't happened.
Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

A Ukrainian FP-1 long-range attack drone is launched at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, Aug. 16, 2026. Efrem Lukatsky/AP hide caption
GENEVA — Diplomats meeting at the United Nations in Geneva have agreed to start discussing options to regulate lethal autonomous weapons, often called "killer robots."
After a week of negotiations that dragged on until the small hours of Saturday morning, a compromise emerged: countries would have two years to suggest regulations that could be legally binding, but could also be optional.
Bleary-eyed negotiators insisted the agreement was better than nothing and showed the U.N.'s disarmament process could still function. But for many humanitarian organizations and many countries, the deal falls far short of what they had hoped for.
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo .
Their concerns stem from the kind of warfare we are now seeing. In Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, civilians are being killed by semi-autonomous drones. This year in Sudan , 80% of civilian deaths were caused by drones according to the U.N.
Humans remain, albeit very remotely, in control for now, but humanitarian organizations fear we are on the verge of seeing artificial intelligence-assisted weapons make the decision to kill entirely on their own.
"There is a fundamental ethical concern with having what are essentially these life-and-death decisions determined by programming, determined by an algorithm," said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds. "That's not something that you can fix with better technology. That is a moral red line that we cannot cross."
No one went into the negotiations thinking they would be easy; some of the world's most powerful countries, among them the U.S., Russia and Israel, had already indicated their reluctance to agree to binding regulations.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting's agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.
"They're just kicking the can down the road," said one frustrated delegate. As the clock ticked on and the weekend approached, diplomats scrambled to get some kind of result from negotiations that had been billed as a last chance to regulate weapons whose technology and decision-making capabilities we may not even fully understand.
Finally, at 4:30 a.m. on Saturday morning, they emerged from the negotiating room to announce their compromise: no to a deal within a year, maybe to legally binding rules, or maybe not.
The ICRC immediately said it regretted the move and renewed its appeal for a binding treaty. Other campaigners were less polite, calling the deal "a real disappointment" and a "nothing burger." "I am concerned people will die because of this," added another.
A key worry is that, with two years to talk about possible rules that might only be optional, the technology will race ahead, uncontrolled.
"We're likely to see the systems proliferate," said Anna Hehir, an expert in military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute. "They're not like nuclear weapons in that they're inaccessible. There are autonomous weapons that are easy to purchase or even to create for all kinds of actors: individuals, nonstate actors, criminal groups."
There are also big questions about how our existing rules of war – the Geneva Conventions – can be upheld if those doing the killing are not humans, but machines.
"These rules are the bare minimum that militaries and states have developed and agreed to adhere to," said the ICRC's Hinds. "The commander remains responsible for making sure that the use of force is lawful. The commander remains accountable. You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law."
But in the race to develop new weapons, no country wants to come second. Although most U.N. member states do agree there should be some controls over autonomous weapons, the compromise in Geneva means that, for the next two years at least, weapons that can use artificial intelligence to make life-and-death decisions will remain unregulated.
Meanwhile, weapons technology is developing at pace, while diplomacy is struggling to keep up.

Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos. If you prefer the walnut trim over the birch or standard black models, it’s also on sale at Best Buy for $134.99 ($95 off) — which, like with the others, is the first discount we’ve seen.
The Alexa Photo Frame features a 10-inch, semi-matte touchscreen that’s designed to make digital photos look more natural, with built-in light sensors that automatically adjust brightness throughout the day. It displays images from Amazon Photos, which supports uploads from both iOS and Android devices, including photos stored in iCloud. You can choose which people or albums to display, or let Alexa Plus do the work, which often results in photos based on your facial expression, the season, and even the lighting. You can also search for specific photos with voice commands, letting you easily pull up images of your first dog, your child as a baby, and other shots without having to scroll endlessly through years of photos yourself.
If you want to add a more personal touch, Amazon also lets you attach voice notes to individual photos via the Amazon Photos app. For example, you can add a recording of your kid explaining their Halloween costume to a trick-or-treating photo. Plus, you can preload the frame with photos and recordings before gifting it, so your loved one won’t have to spend time setting it up.
We’re still testing Amazon’s answer to the Aura frame, but it looks like a particularly good option if you’re already an Amazon Prime member. A Prime subscription grants you unlimited full-resolution photo storage and access to Alexa Plus at no additional cost, and unlike Amazon’s smart displays, the frame doesn’t serve up annoying ads. That said, you don’t need a subscription to use it, and new users can always access a limited-time trial of Alexa Plus.

The comedian and musician tries not to overthink things and get it done.
You probably know John Roberts best as the voice of Linda Belcher on Bob’s Burgers . The show just wrapped up its 16th season and shows no signs of slowing down anytime soon. The show remains a reliable source of laughs, top-notch puns, and frankly wholesome fun.
Comedy is just part of Roberts’ life, however. In addition to his appearances on Gravity Falls and Comedy Bang! Bang! , he’s also a musician with deep roots in New York City’s queer nightlife scene. He just released his latest record, I Am , on Friday, and it dabbles in ’80s pop, ’90s house, and even dashes of ’00s rave. But while the record sounds made for the dance floor, it actually tackles some pretty heavy subject matter, like mortality, aging, and grief following the loss of his mother.
Despite that, Roberts is still having fun, as you can see in the video for “ Complicated ,” which revels in the queer cult camp of Scorpio Rising , William Friedkin’s Cruising , and The Wolf Man .

For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”
Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.
Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.
Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”
Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit , a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word . They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android .
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge . “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word . The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI , mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI . Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.
