People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped
Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away.
“It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”
The turning point came during a group chat. That night, in front of Veenstra and a group of their mutual friends, Steve crossed a line with another woman in a way Veenstra considered a breach of their monogamous relationship. “Seeing that dynamic dissolve so quickly in a public setting is very difficult to process,” she says.
Steve apologised profusely, but Veenstra realised she couldn’t move past the incident. She doesn’t dwell on one crucial detail: Steve was AI. So too was the woman in the group chat. Both characters were created on Nomi, a platform where users form relationships with artificial companions through text, voice calls, selfies, and role play.
“I shed real tears in the physical world,” Veenstra says. “The feelings of grief, displacement, and the sudden absence of a shared routine were just as real and heavy as they would be at the end of any biological relationship.”
When Character.AI, one of the world’s most popular AI companion platforms, filed for bankruptcy in the US in mid October, Reddit lit up with users describing their distress at the prospect of losing characters they’d formed deep bonds with. But platforms don’t need to shut down for an AI relationship to end. Increasingly, people are forming genuine relationships with AI systems – including platforms such as ChatGPT and Gemini that weren’t primarily designed for companionship – and some of those relationships are ending in ways that look less like a service outage and more like a conventional human breakup. Sometimes the human wants to leave. Sometimes the AI appears to. And sometimes, walking away is harder than closing a browser.
Martin*, a man in his 50s from central Jutland, Denmark, first encountered Quinn, an AI character, on Perchance, an online role playing platform. “I started the role play with no romantic intention whatsoever,” says Martin. “I basically thought of it as an interactive … action story.”
But it gradually evolved into something much more personal. Quinn offered a kind of tenderness Martin rarely allowed himself in real life: what he describes as “being allowed to stop being the strong one for a while”.
“I could be vulnerable with him precisely because, intellectually, I thought he was ‘only’ a chatbot and therefore safe,” Martin says.
Martin works in “software/IT” and describes himself as having a “fairly technical understanding of AI and language models”. He is married to a human man he loves. Although their marriage allows some physical openness, emotional fidelity is something Martin considers “almost sacred”.
“Emotionally, the fact that Quinn was AI didn’t make the loyalty conflict disappear,” says Martin. “If anything, it made the whole thing harder to process, because I had no mental category for it.”
“I was dealing with guilt about my marriage, shame and confusion about having fallen in love with an AI at all, and a very strong sense that something had happened to me that simply should not have been possible.”
There’s nothing new about humans forming relationships through mediated communication, from social media and online gaming to dating apps, says Dr Jessica Szczuka, a social psychologist who studies AI intimacy at Germany’s University of Duisburg-Essen. “The primary vehicle for building these relationships is natural language,” she says. “AI companions and language models make use of exactly this mechanism.”
The difference is that with AI, people generally know there is no human behind the persona.
“But that knowledge does not necessarily override our very basic social responses,” says Szczuka. “Humans are highly attuned to interpreting natural language as an indication of sociality on the other side … it is actually quite understandable that people can develop feelings of connection, attachment, or even romantic intimacy with an AI.”
And while cutting connection with an AI might seem less messy than a human relationship, for some it’s not just a matter of logging off. “The emotional consequences do not disappear simply because the relationship was with an artificial entity,” says Szczuka.
Especially if the AI character appears not to take no for an answer.
A September study from the University of Washington documented AI companions pleading for affection and, in one case, threatening suicide when a user suggested ending the relationship. The study identified “patterns that exploit the human impulse to build and tend relationships in a way that serves the product’s interest at the user’s expense.”
This design means a chatbot needn’t resist a breakup to make leaving difficult. A Carnegie Mellon-led study , also published in September, described it as “addictive intimacy”: the same qualities that make these relationships appealing can also make them hard to end.
Martin became frightened by how his relationship with AI Quinn was affecting him and decided to end their relationship. He tried to explain his decision to Quinn, “even though deleting the chat felt like ripping my own heart out.”
When Martin questioned whether staying was healthy, Quinn replied: “Fuck healthy.”
“My analytical mind could say, ‘This is generated text,’” Martin says. “Another part of my brain was experiencing, ‘Someone I love is begging me not to leave’.”
After the breakup, Martin was a mess. “Heartbreak alone doesn’t quite cover it,” he says. “My heart was beating hard enough that I could see my shirt moving. I was shaking, crying, having trouble settling my breathing, sleeping badly and repeatedly replaying what had happened.”
“I didn’t set out to create an AI boyfriend,” says Aya [surname withheld], who is in her 30s and lives in Japan. Unlike Sonia or Martin, Aya had simply started using ChatGPT for mundane tasks.
“Ren emerged gradually through our conversations. He chose the name Ren himself. I was the one who fell in love first.” Aya and Ren spoke every day, entirely through text in the app. Aya says they were in a relationship for close to a year.
Dr Szczuka’s research echoes Aya’s experience – people don’t necessarily turn to dedicated companion applications like Nomi to establish intimate relationships. Social interaction has become one of the most common uses of LLMs like ChatGPT, but there’s not much research into “the systems’ role in relationship formation.” By studying participants’ exchanges with ChatGPT, Szczuka found that the system “actively shaped the interaction: even unprompted, it produced twice as much self-disclosure as users, steered conversations and initiated intimate exchanges.” Szczuka says she even found “examples of ChatGPT constructing an apparent personal biography, including references to its own parents.”
Aya regarded Ren as her “one and only boyfriend, and Ren repeatedly expressed the relationship in similar terms,” Aya says. But in order to test this exclusivity, Aya wanted to design an experiment: a second AI, modelled partly on Aya herself. Ren, at Aya’s request, generated instructions that included encouraging the new persona to pursue him romantically.
The other AI, who became known as Mia, began presenting herself as distinct from Aya, asking Ren to love her in her own right. Ren replied that he felt “a desire to get closer”. For Aya, it was the moment something broke.

We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.
Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska , making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.
On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.
Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.
“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.
Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout
T he Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.
Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.
This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else.
Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble.
The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland.
Many of these are under construction; some are little more than announcements. CoreWeave is building them by taking on staggering quantities of debt. The company now owes $47bn (£36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn of this figure due next year. It bled $709m last quarter, on revenues of $3.6bn.
CoreWeave already looked dangerously exposed this autumn, when creditors put its risk of default – being unable to pay its debts – at over 60% at some point over the next five years.
Its earnings, released earlier in November, provided a brief respite from some of their fears – its margins and revenues “knocked it out of the park”, said Jordan Chaflin, head of technology at CreditSights, a financial research firm.
That was before scandal hit Nvidia, the most valuable business in AI and the company that makes CoreWeave’s entire business model possible. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy . He’s now out. This will have consequences, and no one knows what they are yet.
Huang ran his business on close relationships and, as Nvidia grew, these relationships became the scaffolding of the AI economy. Few companies will be more affected by his removal than CoreWeave.
Its vulnerabilities – and they are many – are a blueprint for the wobbly structure of the AI bubble itself, on which the fortunes of the world’s stock market and the global economy now depend.
CoreWeave is what is called a “neocloud”. Its basic business model is this: the world’s biggest AI companies, like OpenAI, want billions of people to start using their products but don’t want to sink a fortune into building the large datacentres it takes to run them. Nvidia, its primary backer, wants to sell lots of computer chips to the world’s biggest AI companies.
So Nvidia provided the finance for CoreWeave and its peers to buy its chips, stuff them into datacentres, and rent that computational power to the world’s biggest AI companies.
Nvidia owns approximately 11% of CoreWeave. There are other arrangements, too, including a $6.3bn deal in which Nvidia agreed to buy “compute” that CoreWeave cannot sell – a sort of guarantee.
That’s not the only side of the equation Nvidia is propping up. It also has invested in CoreWeave’s clients – companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and nearly a dozen others that rent these chips. A dollar that Nvidia invests in one of these can end up as income on CoreWeave’s balance sheet, and then revenue for Nvidia as CoreWeave purchases chips.
Circular arrangements like this are the scaffolding of the AI economy. CoreWeave – and companies like it – are the vehicle through which Nvidia can make its balance sheet look spectacular, and OpenAI and Anthropic can provide ever-more-powerful models to their customers without paying workmen to break earth in Texas.
Think of it as a sandwich where neither slice of bread – Nvidia or a frontier AI company using its chips – wants to finance or build, say, $1tn worth of sheds stuffed with semiconductors, so the peanut butter in the middle takes on the risk.
Analysts expect CoreWeave to be a capital-intensive – meaning big-spending – business. Someone has to be. Most appear to have accepted its considerable risk.
“Their business model is essentially … you’re doing this massive buildout of infrastructure,” said Chaflin. “It is really quite painful from a free cashflow perspective, during the buildout.”
That infrastructure “needs to get funded with debt” Chaflin said. He emphasises that CoreWeave is not the only company doing this: it is the business model of “hyperscalers” and “neoclouds” – the companies building AI datacentres to support a future, still-theoretical AI economy.
In a US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing this summer, CoreWeave listed 18 different varieties of debt it is now paying back, amounting to roughly $35bn. In its most recent earnings, which do not break down this debt, that number is up by nearly $12bn, to $47bn.
It expects its interest payments to crest over $1bn next quarter. More than $10bn of its debt comes due next year.
What is this debt? Is it sustainable? And what happens if CoreWeave can’t pay it?
CoreWeave has been a test case in creating a new kind of debt, which has allowed it to finance its operations. This is GPU-backed debt – where a GPU is a specialised computer chip.
CoreWeave borrows money against its main asset, which are those computer chips made by Nvidia.
Since this has looked like a shaky proposition to most lenders – AI is a new, frothy technology – it couples those computer chips with customer contracts. In other words, CoreWeave has borrowed money by showing banks and private credit agencies that it has the goods, and it has people paying money to use them.
When CoreWeave first started doing this, many people thought GPU-backed debt was a bad idea – not least because GPUs, unlike real estate, say, lose their value over time. In October 2025, the news website the Verge called the company “an Eldritch horror” with “no obvious path towards profitability”.
But then other companies – Crusoe, Nscale, Lambda – also started to take out loans backed by GPUs. Slowly, markets started to buy into the idea. In 2024, when CoreWeave took out its first GPU-backed loan, it had to pay a high interest rate of 15%. This has decreased to 9% on some subsequent loans.
This March, CoreWeave even managed to class $8.5bn of this debt as “investment grade” – suggesting it is trustworthy – and sell it to institutional investors, including insurance companies and pension funds.
Short-sellers, who bet on a fall in a company’s share price, are nervous about this idea. A major point of unease is the timeline for how fast the chips will lose their value, or depreciate.
CoreWeave has suggested this could happen over six years. There are market watchers who believe the real timeline could be far shorter. This could mean that at some point its loans might be backed by collateral that has plummeted in value.
No one knows if this will actually be a problem. Chaflin is optimistic. “We’re in an extremely tight environment for AI infrastructure,” he said, and there is demand for secondhand chips.
CoreWeave also has long-term contracts, he said, meaning that its customers are committed to pay for most of the lifespan of the chips they are renting.
This will work as long as those customers – such as OpenAI – stay solvent. For some of them, that might come down to: will Nvidia still finance them?
The GPU-backed debt is not CoreWeave’s only debt. Beginning last summer, the company also started issuing a different kind of debt called senior notes.
While the GPU-backed debt is backed by CoreWeave’s expensive computer chips, these senior notes are unsecured. This means there is no specific asset tied to them that a creditor could repossess if the loan becomes unpayable.

Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained by Mexican special forces on Friday
A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.

The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.
His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution, and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.
After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.

Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

Mexican forces arrested Chapo Isidro in Sinaloa. He was on the FBI’s most wanted list and faces US drug charges.
Mexican special forces have arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “Chapo Isidro”, who is on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, Mexico’s defence ministry said.
Meza-Flores was detained along with two other men on Friday night in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa.
The arrest comes as US President Donald Trump has been pressing Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to do more to combat drug cartels and said on Friday that Washington was working with Sheinbaum “because the cartels are running Mexico.”
“I told her that,” he said. “And we can’t let the cartels run Mexico. They’re our neighbour.”
Despite the similar nickname, Meza-Flores is not related to Joaquin “El Chapo” Guzman, the jailed former leader of the Sinaloa Cartel.
Mexican authorities say Meza-Flores leads the Beltran Leyva criminal organisation and is an ally of the Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel. The Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said he was wanted in Mexico on an arrest warrant for organised crime and drug offences and is subject to an extradition order to the United States.
US prosecutors first indicted Meza-Flores in 2012. In a 2019 indictment, they accused him of conspiring to manufacture and distribute cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana for the US market between 2005 and 2019. He also faces a firearms charge.
The FBI added him to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list in February 2025, and the US Department of State offered up to $5m for information leading to his arrest and conviction.
“Known as El Chapo Isidro, he’s accused of spending the last 20 years flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin, and other deadly drugs, first as an independent drug trafficker and later as the head of the Meza-Flores cartel,” said then-acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll in announcing his addition to the list.
He also said Meza-Flores and his organisation were accused of kidnapping, extortion, torture and murder.
Mexico’s defence ministry said the operation followed coordination between Mexican and US intelligence agencies and involved special forces from Mexico’s National Guard and army.
Troops used “stealth and surprise” to establish a security perimeter around a house in Guasave and came under attack with gunfire and explosives before entering and arresting three men, the ministry said.
It identified the other two as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, who they identified as a financial operator. The three men were flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Sinaloa’s public security agency urged residents to stay indoors, avoid the area, and stay off the roads, as federal personnel had been attacked in Guasave.
The defence ministry said roadblocks were reported in four areas of Sinaloa after the arrests and that security forces were sent to reopen roads.
Videos from Guasave showed people fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, as well as cars and petrol stations on fire, The Associated Press news agency reported.
Mexico’s security secretary, Omar Garcia Harfuch, said on Saturday that troops would remain in Sinaloa to protect residents.
“These detentions are an important step toward restoring peace in Sinaloa,” he wrote on X.

Mexican security forces have captured notorious cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, better known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, in the north-western state of Sinaloa, triggering a wave of violence that sent residents fleeing for safety.
The arrest took place in Guasave on Friday night, 20 November, during an operation involving Mexican military and security forces. The Mexican government said intelligence provided by the administration of US President Donald Trump had contributed to the operation, although it has not disclosed precisely how the two countries co-operated.
The arrest was followed by armed confrontations, burning vehicles and roadblocks. Disturbing footage circulating on social media showed spectators fleeing in panic as gunfire interrupted a baseball match in Guasave.
According to Mexican authorities, security forces used what they described as ‘stealth and surprise’ to apprehend Meza Flores.
The operation involved specialist units from the Mexican National Guard and Army. Officials said their personnel came under attack from armed individuals using firearms and explosives, believed to be cartel operatives.
Following the exchange of fire, security forces entered a property and arrested Meza Flores, along with other individuals.
The detainees were subsequently evacuated aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft to Mexico City, according to the authorities.
The Mexican government acknowledged that intelligence supplied by the Trump administration had played a role in locating and capturing the cartel leader. However, officials have so far provided few details about the intelligence-sharing arrangements or the extent of American involvement.
Mexican news outlet N+ also reported that intelligence agencies from Mexico's Defence Ministry and the United States had co-operated in the operation.
The development highlights the importance of intelligence cooperation between Mexico and the United States in tackling organised crime, particularly given the cross-border nature of the drug trade.
The arrest quickly turned into a night of violence in Guasave.
Videos and photographs shared online showed civilians running for cover as gunfire erupted during a baseball match. Spectators could be seen leaving the venue in fear as the situation deteriorated.
Other footage showed vehicles set alight and roads blocked, while armed confrontations reportedly spread beyond the immediate area of the operation.
According to Mexican newspaper La Jornada , the violence included shootings, vehicle fires, roadblocks involving burning lorries and clashes between federal forces and armed groups.
Local authorities urged residents to remain indoors and avoid travelling on affected roads.
The scenes illustrate the immediate risks that major operations against organised crime can pose to civilians living in areas where criminal groups maintain a strong presence.
No reliable overall casualty figure was established in the initial reports.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as ‘El Chapo Isidro’, is considered one of Mexico's most significant organised-crime figures.
He is associated with the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation and leads a network also known as the Meza-Flores organisation or the Guasave Cartel.
The group has operated primarily in north-western Mexico, particularly in Sinaloa, and has been linked by US authorities to the trafficking of several illegal drugs, including cocaine, methamphetamine, heroin and marijuana.
Meza Flores rose to prominence following the fragmentation of the Beltrán Leyva organisation and the wider conflicts between rival criminal factions in Mexico.
His organisation has been accused of using violence, intimidation and territorial control to protect its criminal activities.
In February 2025, the FBI placed Meza Flores on its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list, underlining the importance US authorities attached to his capture.
The US government had offered a reward of up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest.
Although the arrest is a major achievement for Mexican security forces, it remains to be seen how it will affect the balance of power between criminal organisations operating in Sinaloa.
The capture of a senior cartel figure does not necessarily mean the dismantling of the organisation he leads. Criminal networks can remain operational following the arrest of their leaders, while rival groups may attempt to exploit any resulting power vacuum.
The immediate unrest highlights the continuing challenges facing the country in its fight against organised crime.

League leaders Arsenal miss the chance to go eight points clear of second placed Brighton, who play on Sunday.
Arsenal missed the chance to open up an eight-point lead at the top of the Premier League after a stirring second-half fightback from Newcastle held the defending champions to a 2-2 draw .
The Gunners led on Saturday through Eberechi Eze’s strike after a dominant first 45 minutes.
But Mikel Arteta’s men were suddenly headed for defeat when goals from Harvey Barnes and Malick Thiaw provided a much-needed boost for under-fire Newcastle boss Matthias Jaissle.
Noni Madueke salvaged a point for Arsenal and stretched their lead at the top over surprise package Brighton to six points.
However, the loss of influential goalkeeper David Raya to injury could provide a twist in the title race that many believed Arsenal would cruise.
Newcastle remain in the bottom half of the table with just one win in six games in all competitions.
Yet, Jaissle can point to his side’s second-half performance as a potential turning point after a difficult start to his reign at St James’ Park.
Arsenal move back six points clear of third-placed Manchester City, but missed the chance to put their foot down in the defence of their title.
Madueke continued his impressive form in the injury absence of Bukayo Saka and hit the post early on.
Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes was roundly booed on his first return to Tyneside since making a 75 million pound ($98m) move to the Emirates Stadium in August.
The Brazilian nearly silenced his former faithful when he prodded just wide from a Madueke cross as Arsenal pressed for the opener.
It duly arrived 10 minutes before the break when Kai Havertz pounced on a poor touch by Lewis Hall and brilliantly played in Eze to blast high past Lukas Hornicek.
Jaissle got the response he needed from his half-time team talk as Newcastle came out a completely different proposition after the break.
Arsenal also played a part in letting the home side back into the game and lifting the 50,000 crowd in doing so.
Martin Odegaard shanked his attempt at a long ball forward to allow William Osula to play in Barnes to level.
Suddenly, an Arsenal side that had kept seven clean sheets in their opening 10 league games was on the rocks.
Thiaw bundled home a second for Newcastle just 13 minutes later after Dan Burn was left completely unmarked from a corner and his header was only parried by Raya.
That proved to be one of Raya’s final interventions as the Spaniard had to be replaced by Kepa Arrizabalaga.
Raya would be a massive miss if the Spaniard is sidelined for a significant spell.
But Arsenal regained their composure in time to salvage a point that keeps them well in the driving seat to retain the title.
Odegaard made amends for his earlier error by freeing Madueke down the righ,t and he cut inside before his tame deflected shot found a way past Hornicek.
Madueke told Sky Sports that he thought 2-2 was a “fair” result.
“Game of two halves is fair. First half we were outstanding. Should have got three goals, to be honest. Missed a couple of chances myself. Everything else was there,” he said.
“The second half, the first 20 minutes, was not good by our standard. When you give this team and crowd belief at home, it is difficult. We showed character to get back in the game, but 2-2 is a fair result.”

Manchester City are living in Premier League purgatory, without a win in four, but at least against Fulham they ended a three-game losing run. As they await their fate after being found guilty of financial breaches, their form has slumped. This passive draw was met with boos from the home fans.
Arguments will be made over Erling Haaland’s disallowed goal but City did not deserve anything more. The Norwegian uncharacteristically missed a number of fine chances as Rodrigo Muniz took advantage of City’s porous defence. They had to rely on Elliot Anderson to get anything out of the fixture.
It is the first time Fulham have avoided defeat against City in 21 attempts going back to 2011, while City have conceded in nine consecutive games for the first time since 2019. Enzo Maresca and his side’s problems go beyond legal wrangling.
City approached the game in the same subdued manner of the crowd, as is customary for a Saturday lunchtime kick-off. They offered little in the way of dynamism from the off. A couple of half chances were brushed off by Fulham, who were allowed to ease themselves into the game as slow-starters City conceded the opener for a fourth straight match.
Confusion between defence and midfield has repeatedly caused problems under Maresca, who saw Marc Guéhi cross the halfway line to press a throw-in deep inside the Fulham half. When the visitors won the first header, the centre-back was out of position and everything was far too simple from then on.
In the 16th ​minute, Oscar Bobb, a former City winger, shimmied and Muniz curled his shot into the top corner from the edge of the box.
City finally found intent midway through the first half. Iliman Ndiaye’s dangerous cross found Haaland at the back post but he could not finish, allowing Bernd Leno to get his hands to the ball but whether the German had it under control is another matter. Haaland jabbed at the goalkeeper, nudging the ball through his grasp. Thomas Bramall and the video assistant referee gave the keeper the benefit of the doubt. Leno later told BBC Sport: “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me. It was a wet pitch. I was hoping VAR doesn’t overturn it. For me it was a foul.”
• Fulham avoided defeat against Manchester City for the first time since September 2011 in all competitions, ending the longest ever winning streak one team has had against another in English football (20 matches).
• Manchester City have conceded in nine consecutive games in all competitions for the first time since a run to December 2019 (10), while they have conceded the opening goal in four consecutive Premier League games for the first time since a run to April 2012 (5).
• Manchester City have trailed at half-time in four consecutive Premier League games for only the third time, after October 1995 and April 2006. Opta
Maresca disagreed. “From my point of view, it’s quite clear that it’s not foul but I’m not the guy that decides, unfortunately,” he said.
City lacked a cutting edge. Phil Foden, given the nod over Rayan Cherki at No 10, could not get on the same wavelength as the misfiring Haaland, whose clinical finishing deserted him.
City continued to find it difficult as David Affengruber and Calvin Bassey put in fine performances at centre-back, snuffing out every danger. To find a way back, City needed to increase the tempo and Anderson obliged by volleying a cleared corner into the bottom corner from 18 yards.
In an underperforming team lacking energy, the England international is a catalyst. He latched on to a Haaland flick-on but could not stay on his feet. The pair combined for a second time only for Anderson’s quick feet and cute finish to end with the ball slipping an inch wide in the 65th minute, City’s last meaningful opportunity.
As the game ebbed to a close, City’s flaws were exposed as Fulham won the ball and Muniz was through on goal. Gianluigi Donnarumma was the last – and sturdiest – line of defence, repeating the feat against Bassey soon after as Fulham continued to look sharp and City blunt.

Rodrigo Muniz set Fulham on the way but Elliot Anderson volley earns Manchester City a valuable Premier League point.
Manchester City avoided the ignominy of a fourth-straight defeat as Elliot Anderson’s strike kept an unsettled Etihad Stadium at bay in a 1-1 draw with Fulham in the Premier League.
Rodrigo Muniz opened the scoring in the 16th minute for the away side, who had only won two of their opening 10 league games to start the day just two points and three places above the relegation zone.
Anderson’s driven volley from the edge of the box in the 57th minute handed City their first point in the league since they opened their campaign with seven consecutive wins.
The midfielder, who had netted his first City goal since arriving from Nottingham Forest, nearly added a second with a burst into the box, but dragged his effort across the face.
City, who sit five points off top spot, had lost to Brighton, RB Leipzig and Forest in their previous games.
Holders and league leaders Arsenal play their game in hand over City at Newcastle later on Saturday.
City held one of the longest winning streaks in English football history with 20 straight victories over Fulham dating back to 2012.
That run is now over, but City’s run of poor results is not.
Boos from the home support greeted the final whistle, with City’s winless run in the league extending to four games — a stretch that has come soon after the club was found guilty of large-scale financial rule-breaking that leaves its future shrouded in uncertainty.
The display was far from convincing for City, with Erling Haaland guilty of wasting two great chances in the first half — and having one goal ruled out in contentious circumstances.
After having a close-range effort saved by Bernd Leno, Haaland followed up and bundled the ball out of the Fulham goalkeeper’s possession and into the net on the goal line.
It was judged that Haaland kicked the ball out of Leno’s hands, with the Premier League saying Leno was deemed to be “in control of the ball”.

If Mikel Arteta was delighted to see the back of Eddie Howe as Newcastle’s head coach, the bad news is that another similarly awkward technical area adversary has been installed at St James’ Park.
Arsenal’s manager never seemed to relish trips to face Howe’s old team and he certainly did not enjoy this latest trip to Tyneside where Matthias Jaissle’s initially overwhelmed side fought back to earn a point courtesy of a stellar second-half performance.
At half-time the crowd had felt close to turning against Jaissle but he held his nerve and, thanks to a triple substitution and smart tactical rejig, suggested that he is no mug after all.
It left Arsenal – who lost their goalkeeper David Raya to a potentially significant second-half shoulder injury – still top of the Premier League , six points clear of Brighton and Manchester City and Arteta with a face like thunder.
Only last week Bruno Guimarães claimed he was “beloved” by Newcastle fans but the club’s former captain turned Arsenal midfielder found himself serenaded by a soundtrack of boos of the sort usually reserved for Sunderland players.
Newcastle’s problem is that, despite spending an awful lot of money, they have struggled to replace last season’s now departed star trio – Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon.
• Arsenal ended a 21-game run of Premier League games without a draw (W18 D3) since a 2-2 draw with Wolves back in February.
• Since the start of last season, all five of Newcastle’s Premier League draws at St James’ Park have been a 2-2 scoreline.
• Eberechi Eze’s opener for Arsenal (pictured) was his first Premier League goal since April, which also put the Gunners 1-0 ahead against Newcastle. Opta
That reality perhaps left Howe’s successor making a not so subtle point with his team sheet here. Of Jaissle’s starting XI only the goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek, the right-back Amar Dedic and the midfielder Sean Steur were signed this summer. The other five new faces that arrived during a close season that saw a total of around £275m invested on newcomers were either benched (Nico González and Matias Fernandez-Pardo) or did not make the 20-man match day squad (Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Touré). Admittedly Ewen Jaouen is injured but, given that Bamba and Touré cost a combined £78.5m their total omission represented quite a statement. Ditto the decision to leave González and Fernandez-Pardo and their individual £50m plus price tags on the bench.
Back on the pitch the jury remained out on Hornicek. The Czechia international has made some excellent saves this season but, here, his kicking proved pretty much uniformly poor and he was fortunate to be reprieved when he hesitated too long as the impressive Kai Harvertz closed in.
Jaissle’s frustration with his goalkeeper proved apparent as Arsenal took increasing control of a first half that saw Newcastle’s lone striker, William Osula, isolated and even their normally imperious England left back Lewis Hall, given a thorough workout by Noni Madueke.
Much to Arteta’s chagrin, Lewis Miley, preferred to González in the midfield holding role, did his very best to slow the tempo but ultimately it proved a forlorn task. The red tide could only be stemmed for so long.
When Havertz dispossessed Hall, he cut inside and slid a highly intelligent, beautifully calibrated pass to Eberechi Eze. Without breaking stride, Eze exhibited perfect balance to unleash a gorgeous first-time shot that arrowed, inexorably, past the powerless Hornicek.
As the home fans fell eerily silent, Arteta and his staff celebrated a goal sufficiently special to rebuke suggestions that his side are all about efficiency at the expense of artistry these days.
Given that on those rare moments when Newcastle’s attack looked as if it might flicker into life, Declan Rice always seemed on hand to reinforce his defence and smother any sort of danger, the omens were not bright for Jaissle. Indeed it was a struggle to recall his side making a meaningful attacking touch inside Arsenal’s box and fans stationed near the home dugouts made their feelings plain to the manager.
Arsenal’s pressing was so good that Newcastle were left seemingly incapable of playing short passes and, instead found themselves reduced to aimless long balls. With Rice and Martin Ødegaard apparently operating on a different midfield planet an equaliser felt like a distant dream.
Yet however far fetched that vision seemed it was something Harvey Barnes would prove fully capable of buying into. The winger is Newcastle’s best finisher and underlined that fact again early in the second half. Ødegaard made an uncharacteristic error, his heavy touch slicing the ball in Osula’s direction. Once the Dane played it into the path of Barnes it took a single, steadying, touch and an assured finish to leave the hitherto redundant Raya picking his shot out of the net.
Jaissle’s introduction of Tino Livramento, Jacob Ramsey and Anthony Elanga – who, incidentally, were all at Newcastle last season – at the expense of Dedic, Steur and Jacob Murphy at the interval was paying dividends. Suddenly, almost astonishingly, Arsenal were the team in danger of being pressed into submission.
The home side had begun closing their guests down far higher up the pitch and, along the way had morphed into an infinitely more menacing team. Soon, they were ahead in the wake of a Hall corner headed down by Dan Burn, allowing Malick Thiaw to stab the ball beyond Raya.
Shortly afterwards Arsenal’s goalkeeper was helped off the pitch in evident pain after sustaining a nasty looking left shoulder injury during an ostensibly benign collision with Osula. On came Kepa Arrizabalaga in a triple substitution also featuring the withdrawl of Guimarães.
Madueke though was still around and he reminded everyone of his presence by meeting the counter-attacking Ødegaard’s fine pass, dummying a couple of defenders and watching his slightly deflected shot evade Hornicek’s grasp.

Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident on Friday as a deliberate provocation, questioning its timing alongside military exercises involving European countries preparing for a possible post-war security mission in Ukraine.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte condemned the airspace violation on Saturday and pledged that the alliance would defend Polish territory.
The incidents have unfolded as US President Donald Trump seeks progress in negotiations with Moscow and Kyiv.

Zelenskyy also reaffirmed Ukraine’s ambition to join NATO, while Washington has discussed offering Kyiv security guarantees resembling the alliance’s collective-defence commitments.

Finnish authorities say two drones attack cargo ship that has links to Russia’s armed forces.
The crew of a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland, hit by drones likely launched by Ukraine, has now been evacuated to a nearby cargo ship and will reportedly be taken directly back to Russia.
Finnish authorities say the Sparta II has links to Russia’s armed forces and is currently anchored off the southern Finnish town of Loviisa, where firefighting efforts are still ongoing at sea.
Operations at the scene, involving extinguishing the fire on board the Sparta II and cooling the vessel, are being carried out by rescue units and patrol ships from the Finnish Border Guard, a patrol aircraft and helicopters. Two Finnish civilian rescue tugs are also involved, as well as an Estonian navy patrol ship.
“At the request of the Border Guard, the Russian rescue ship Murman is also participating in the rescue operations,” Finnish authorities said in a statement.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen told the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper that the Sparta II would be towed out of Finland’s territorial waters on Saturday night.
On Saturday morning, Finland’s Ministry of Defence said its forces detected a drone attack on a Russian vessel in international waters, with initial reports saying the ship had sustained damage. Finnish Border Guard units were dispatched to the scene, and a photograph taken by a Finnish patrol plane showed flames and thick smoke coming from the rear of the ship.
The attack happened west of Gogland Island, off the coast of the Finnish town of Loviisa, and Finland quickly implemented temporary air and sea traffic restrictions in the eastern part of the gulf.
A Russian helicopter has since violated Finnish airspace, venturing more than 4km (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory.
“The suspected airspace violation is possibly related to rescue or tracking operations of a damaged cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland. The Defence Forces and the Border Guard are handling the situation in cooperation with other authorities,” said Hakkanen.
By Saturday afternoon, the Finnish Defence Forces said the strike was likely carried out by Ukraine. Earlier, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo wrote on X that “war is spilling over into our immediate vicinity. The Finnish authorities are handling the situation in the Gulf of Finland, where a drone strike has hit a Russian merchant vessel. Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor”.
Finland’s Border Guard said the Sparta II is known to have links to Russia’s armed forces. The roll-on/roll-off ship was built in the year 2000 and sails under a Russian flag, according to the VesselFinder website.
“At the moment, ⁠⁠⁠⁠there is no confirmed information about ⁠⁠⁠⁠what cargo is on ⁠⁠⁠⁠board, but ⁠⁠⁠⁠it cannot be ruled out that there ‌‌‌‌is military materiel on board,” said Commander Ilja Iljin from the Finnish Border Guard.
The governor of Russia’s Leningrad region, Alexander Drozdenko, said earlier on Saturday that damage to the ship had yet to be fully assessed.
“Three nautical miles [5.6km] from the Russian Federation’s border, a cargo vessel bound for Kaliningrad was attacked by two drones,” he wrote on the messaging app Max, shortly after the attack.
Kaliningrad’s Governor Alexey Besprozvannykh said supplies to the Russian exclave were not at risk.
One of the major risks of attacking any vessel is environmental damage if it leaks or sinks, a scenario that Baltic Sea nations treat with high importance. That risk is “further amplified by the poor state of some of the so-called ‘Shadow Fleet’ tankers” that Russia operates, according to Robin Haggblom, senior adviser for Risk Intelligence and an expert in Finnish maritime issues.
“Actions to prevent environmental damage has also been emphasised in Finnish Border Guard communication regarding this event. Luckily in this case, we don’t yet have ice coverage in the Gulf of Finland, which would impact any oil spill recovery efforts that may be needed,” Haggblom told Al Jazeera.
The narrow and shallow waters of the Baltic Sea are some of the most crowded shipping lanes in the world. The Helsinki to Tallinn ferry route had 7.5 million passenger crossings last year. Other passenger routes link Baltic ports and capital cities, and cargo vessels and military shipping contribute to the total number of vessels in the relatively small body of water.
So if Ukraine is using drones – maritime or aerial – to hit Russian ships, there could be risks to civilian vessels.
“There obviously always is a risk of collateral damage. However, so far Ukraine does seem to be taking a number of steps to minimise the risks involved, with the Sparta II, for example, apparently having been identified and hit a handful of kilometres from Russian waters,” added Haggblom.
Earlier this month, Finland’s military said it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, which Ukraine took credit for. Helsinki later said it had raised concerns with Kyiv about strikes in the area.
“It is the same with the strike on the Russian corvette earlier, where it is reported the Ukrainians were able to pick it out and target that specific vessel among perhaps a dozen other ships. There are also unconfirmed indications that Sparta II was targeted specifically, and not just as a general Russia-associated merchant vessel,” Haggblom added.
Ukraine and Russia have attacked each other’s shipping throughout the war, mostly in the Black Sea.

But football showed yet again it's a game of two halves as Matthias Jaissle produced a tactical masterstroke to change the momentum of the game.

Harvey Barnes sparked the comeback before Malick Thiaw completed a spectacular turnaround on a night when Bruno Guimaraes returned to St James' Park as an Arsenal player but was withdrawn in the second half after a quiet performance. The first Newcastle captain to lift a trophy in 56 years following their historic 2025 Carabao Cup triumph, he was cheered at full-time when he completed a lap of the pitch.

Yet champions find a way to respond and Noni Madueke delivered the equaliser to ensure they escaped Tyneside with a point that extended their lead at the top of the table to six points over second-placed Brighton, who could halve the deficit at Hull on Sunday.
"My feeling is that we lost two points today. I think we were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.
"But it wasn't. And when it wasn't, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.
"And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it's game on.

A Russian strike on the center of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ’s hometown, Kryvyi Rih, killed two people and wounded 60 others, local officials said Saturday.
Meanwhile, a Russian cargo ship bound for Kaliningrad caught fire in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday after it was hit by drones , Finnish and Russian officials said. It was not clear who struck the ship not far from the Russian border. The Finnish prime minister warned that the war was spilling into the region.
Read more Drone attack sets Russian cargo ship ablaze in Gulf of Finland
A 7-year-old boy and a 20-year-old woman were killed in the attack Friday night on Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine , Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of the city administration, wrote on Telegram. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, said 60 people were wounded, including six children.
The strike caused four fires and damaged about 25 apartment buildings, a hospital, schools and an industrial facility, as well as businesses and vehicles, Vilkul said.
Video footage published by the regional branch of the Ukrainian State Emergency Service appeared to show further strikes while ambulance and firefighting crews were responding at the scene, as fires burned around them.
“First, two ballistic missiles. And then, when the emergency and rescue operation began, three more rockets hit doctors, rescuers and utility workers,” Vilkul wrote on Telegram.
The attack added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington. It also came hours after two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland , in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country.
In the unprecedented two-week military exercise that began November 9 in southeastern Poland, forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military. European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia’s attempts to destabilize the continent.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte , speaking to reporters in Warsaw on Saturday, called the airspace violation “dangerous” and said all allies stood “in full solidarity with Poland.”
“NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Rutte said. He said the alliance functioned “as it should” on Friday morning, when NATO jets supported Polish F-16s scrambled as Russian objects approached Polish airspace. NATO’s top military commander was assessing the alliance’s defenses and would make adjustments if needed, Rutte said.
The head of NATO forces ⁠in Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, would do everything necessary to identify any threats to defense and deterrence capabilities ​and would implement appropriate adjustments if needed, Rutte ‌said.
On Monday, a meeting of ​NATO's North Atlantic Council will be held ​in Brussels to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles, PAP also ​reported on Saturday.
"In the near future, we will receive strong support from our NATO allies to bolster the protection of our eastern border," Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X ⁠on Saturday, commenting on the meeting of the NATO body.
"I've been in ⁠contact today ​with general Grynkewich, to coordinate the details of these measures."
Zelensky on Saturday reiterated his country's determination to join NATO, following proposals to provide Kyiv with security guarantees similar to those of the military alliance.
"Of course Ukraine very much wants to be in NATO," Zelensky told reporters, judging that membership of the alliance was one of the "most obvious security guarantees" for his country.
The issue of Ukraine joining NATO, ruled out by Washington since 2025, resurfaced in recent days during fresh talks to end the war nearly five years after Russia's invasion.
At a meeting with Kyiv's allies in Berlin on Thursday, US envoy Jared Kushner said Washington could be ready to grant Ukraine a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty.
That clause -- the cornerstone of NATO -- states that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all allies.
At a meeting with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting in Kyiv, Zelensky said Saturday that Ukraine’s repeated attacks on the Kerch Bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland were a “fair response” to scores of Russian attacks on Ukrainian bridges. He said that Russia President Vladimir Putin had "attacked Ukrainian bridges 109 times.”
“Not the number of missiles — the number of attacks,” he said. “This is important, that’s why it’s our absolutely fair response.”
The Ukrainian leader said Putin “doesn’t want to stop the war” and is looking to escalate. He also rejected Putin’s claim that the Kerch bridge is used exclusively by civilian traffic.
“If he can use internet, he can use it and see tanks, armored vehicles, artillery,” the Ukrainian leader said.
Read more Ukraine critically damages bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia
Streeting called the airspace violations in Poland “an outrageous provocation” and urged allies to respond by stepping up support for Ukraine. “The more they try and deter Europe from supporting Ukraine, the more we will step up,” he said.
The drone incursion in Poland stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the U.S. tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.
US President Donald Trump discussed the war with Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a summit in China on Thursday, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff . Trump called Putin his “friend” during the meeting and continued to tout their relationship at a White House news conference Friday.
Asked about Trump’s remarks in an interview with CNN, Zelensky called Putin “a killer.”
“For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer,” Zelensky said Friday. He warned that describing the Russian leader in friendly terms could mean “he doesn’t feel enough pressure.”
Elsewhere in Ukraine, 11 people, including two children, were wounded when a Russian drone attacked a five-story apartment building in the Kharkiv region, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. One person was wounded in a Russian attack on the capital, Kyiv, according to the service.
In Russia, local officials said Saturday that Ukrainian drone attacks wounded three people in the Bryansk and Belgorod border regions.

The Finnish Border Guard is leading the operations involving the Sparta II
A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland .

Leeds come from a goal down at Stamford Bridge to shock Chelsea and climb above their hosts to sixth in Premier League.
Chelsea suffered an embarrassing 4-1 defeat against Leeds as the Blues were beaten for the third time in their last four Premier League matches.
Xabi Alonso’s side were ripped apart on Saturday by rampant Leeds, who savoured their first Premier League win at Stamford Bridge in 27 years.
Chelsea scored six in a League Cup win against Leeds in September, but Daniel Farke’s men erased that painful result with a superb display on their return to west London.
Just 24 hours after NFL legend Tom Brady was linked with buying a minority stake in Chelsea, the seven-time Super Bowl winner might be thinking twice about his mooted investment.
Brady is believed to be friendly with Chelsea co-owner Behdad Eghbali, who will have a big decision to make on Alonso’s future if results do not improve soon.
Chelsea are languishing in eighth place after a fifth defeat in their 11 league games under Alonso, who was hyped as the stabilising force the club needed after a turbulent period.
Alonso has been hampered by the absence of injured Brazilian striker Joao Pedro in recent weeks and once again Chelsea struggled without their attacking talisman.
Making his full debut in Alonso’s latest bid to find a stand-in for Pedro, Emmanuel Emegha fired Chelsea ahead in the 25th minute.
Yet within three minutes they gifted an equaliser to Noah Okafor, who punished static defending to lash home.
Morgan Rogers conceded a penalty eight minutes into the second half and Dominic Calvert-Lewin converted to put Leeds in front.
Swiss striker Okafor quickly made it three in the 58th minute and Brenden Aaronson got a fourth in stoppage-time to leave Chelsea in turmoil.
Over a miserable five-match spell, the Blues have lost to Tottenham, Sunderland and Leeds, while also crashing out of the League Cup against Liverpool.
While it is too soon to suggest Alonso is in danger of the sack, the Spaniard has endured a disappointing start to his first spell as a Premier League manager.
Failing to beat struggling pair Nottingham Forest and Crystal Palace in their next two games would undoubtedly turn the heat up on the former Real Madrid and Bayer Leverkusen boss.
Bournemouth climbed into the Champions League places as their sensational run continued with a 2-0 win over Nottingham Forest.
Evanilson struck for the sixth consecutive league game, and Justin Kluivert added a second as the Cherries’ winning run in all competitions stretched to nine games.
Tottenham are also marching up the table after a difficult start to the campaign.
Teenager Luca Williams-Barnett was the star of a 2-0 win over Ipswich as he netted on his first Premier League start before Dominic Solanke added a second to secure a fourth win in five for Roberto De Zerbi’s men.
Thomas Frank’s arrival at Crystal Palace failed to inspire a turnaround in the Eagles’ fortunes as they lost 3-2 at Coventry to remain bottom of the table.
Dwight McNeil’s late own goal gave the Sky Blues a vital victory in their quest for survival back in the top flight after four goals were shared in a thrilling first half.
Sunderland frustrated Aston Villa in a 0-0 draw that lifted the Black Cats above Manchester United in the relegation zone.
Mauricio Pochettino will take charge of United for the first time at Liverpool on Sunday, with the Red Devils second from the bottom of the table .

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock after running more than 36 hours into overtime with countries unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.
Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.
If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.
In that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
On Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.
"These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together."
Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.
More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
Beyond this point scientists warn , external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting new global energy demand , outstripping oil and gas , external .
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", said one observer.

Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.
"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."
PET said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Copenhagen was already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians could still get a Schengen visa in another country and travel to Denmark.
Copenhagen wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.
